title: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Nevertheless I cannot doubt that this process, continued during centuries, would improve and modify any breed, in the same way as Bakewell, Collins, etc., by this very same process, only carried on more methodically, did greatly modify, even during their own lifetimes, the forms and qualities of their cattle.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Methodical and Unconscious Selection”. Scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selection response is testable, but classifying it as unconscious and extending it to any breed require records that mostly do not exist. Existing data support selected case studies.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use historical pedigrees, phenotypes and genomes to test whether preferential reproduction of higher-performing individuals predicts directional breed change despite no formal breeding goal. Sustained response matching selection differentials supports the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Long time series with both parent choice and phenotype are rare.

Intentions of historical breeders are unobserved.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.38
discriminating power: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The process can be approximated with long phenotypic series under weak selection, but public breed systems do not encode intent or century-scale pedigrees. Landrace collections and breed lists support only a static proxy. Environment and methodical selection remain tangled with any trend that can be assembled from papers and herd books.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track phenotypic or breeding-value change in populations where the recorded practice was only 'breed from the best animals' without a written improvement target, over multi-decade to century scales, and compare the direction of change with methodical breeding programmes. Sustained change in the preferred direction under the weaker practice would support the claim; stasis once methodical goals are absent would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Nutrition, climate, and market standards change the phenotype in parallel with any breeding choice.

Open breed databases do not store century-long individual pedigrees tied to selection criteria.

Historical records rarely label a breeding practice as unconscious rather than methodical.
